business.title: Explainable IoT intrusion detection via bio-inspired encoding and interpretable AI models
business.description: We introduce an explainable Internet of Things (IoT) intrusion detection framework built on a bio-inspired Amino Acid encoding of network flows. The flow features are first transformed with the Yeo–Johnson transformation, the most informative ones are selected, and their values are encoded as Amino Acid sequences, which are then summarized by ten protein structural properties (e.g., $$\beta $$-Turn, Isoelectric Point and Molecular Weight). In this way every flow is described by the same compact set of ten properties, whatever the feature set of the original dataset. The models are explained with SHAP, LIME and ELI5, complemented by Captum Integrated Gradients and Alibi anchors for the neural models, and the attributions are linked back to the raw traffic features through measured correlations. On a balanced 50,000-flow subset of CICIoT2023 that covers all 33 attack classes, most of the 12 classical and 5 deep models reach 98.4–98.5% accuracy on a held-out test set (MCC up to 0.97). The recurrent neural network (RNN), used for the in-depth explainability study, reaches 98.5% accuracy with a false-alarm rate of 0.02%, has fewer than 15,000 parameters and needs about 0.1 ms per flow on a CPU. An ablation experiment shows that encoding the selected features keeps detection close to the full 39-feature raw representation (MCC 0.970 against 0.979), while giving a fixed ten-property input that can be explained. All explanation methods agree that $$\beta $$-Turn and Isoelectric Point drive most decisions, and both properties correlate strongly with the packet count and packet size of the flows.

science.title: Antimicrobial activity of apramycin formulated with dextran-based single-chain polymeric nanoparticles against Acinetobacter baumannii
science.description: The global emergence of antimicrobial resistance is driving the development of novel strategies for treating bacterial infections. In this context, dextran-based single-chain polymeric nanoparticles (DXT-SCPNs) have been developed as antibiotic delivery systems for the treatment of pulmonary infections. A series of DXT-SCPNs were formulated with apramycin with different physicochemical properties, namely three degrees of substitution (with a low degree of crosslinking in all cases): low (L-DSa), medium (M-DSa), or high (H-DSa), and two degrees of crosslinking (with a medium degree of substitution in both nanoparticles): low (M-DSa) or high (H-CLa). Their in vitro activity against eleven Acinetobacter baumannii clinical isolates was assessed compared to the free drug, using minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) and time-kill kinetic (TKK) assays. Overall, no statistically significant differences were observed between the antimicrobial activity of free and formulated apramycin. Nevertheless, a slight trend towards higher activity was observed in the cases of M-DSa and H-CLa.

science.title: Leonid meteor shower brings fast-moving shooting stars
science.description: Saskatchewan residents will have another opportunity to watch for shooting stars this November as the annual Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak around Nov. 17-18. Known for their exceptionally fast-moving meteors, the Leonids are among the more recognizable annual meteor showers. Although they do not always produce large numbers of shooting stars, their speed and occasional spectacular displays make them worth watching. science.title: Assessment of potential bias mechanisms in the analysis of large electronic medical record datasets
science.description: Electronic medical records aid general practitioners in the follow-up of their patients. The vast amounts of patient data that are being collected through such electronic medical records offer opportunities to use them for other purposes such as epidemiological and (pre)clinical research. But the use of electronic medical record data for research purposes raises concerns about potential biases, since these data are typically not collected within a study design specifically developed to address a predefined research question, which may instead emerge during or after data collection. In addition, data collection practices and reporting behaviours can vary between general practitioners, while patients themselves differ in their likelihood of seeking care or reporting symptoms. Although a large patient population may mitigate some of these random variations through the law of large numbers, systematic biases related to the non-randomized sample of the participating practices and heterogeneity in patient characteristics may persist. If not appropriately accounted for, these sources of heterogeneity and potential bias can lead to different or potentially conflicting research findings. Using a large electronic medical records dataset from Flanders, Belgium, we assess how simple statistical approaches, such as adding practice-level random effects and changing the analytical entity, can help identify potential bias mechanisms and assess the sensitivity of estimated associations to them.
